jokes.punchline: Three words, apparently relating to something that happened offscreen during the lockout. The specificity of 'a man' (not 'someone,' not 'him') suggests she doesn't know who, which raises more questions than it answers
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum mystery. The gap between confession and context is never filled, which is funnier than any explanation could be. 'A man' is the right indefinite article — it implies Britta encountered a stranger in the Colorado mountains and slapped him, which raises enormous unanswered questions. Perfect Britta absurdism. The timing (after the poop confession, as an additional revelation) makes it land even harder. One of the episode's most quotable lines.

jokes.text: The post-credits scene: Blake's voicemail — 'Hi, this is Blake, the gentleman to whom you're selling the giant hand... it's Blake with a B, the purchaser of the giant hand. Bye.' — followed by the reveal that Blake is a lonely man who bought a giant watch and his wife is leaving him
jokes.setup: Post-credits cold scene: a stranger (Blake) has been waiting for the giant hand to be delivered; we meet him and his wife
jokes.punchline: Blake has also been buying giant versions of everyday objects to cope with the disappearance of his son (who floated away on a giant kite), and his wife announces she's 'going to walk the dog, and eventually leave you'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional cold tag. The episode's MacGuffin (the giant hand) is revealed to be one man's grief object — he gave his son a giant kite, the son disappeared (presumably floating away), and now he compulsively buys giant objects hoping one will bring him back. 'He's waiting for a better daddy, with a bigger hand' is genuinely dark. 'I'll put the watch in the garage. And probably stop showering.' is a perfect button on the Blake character. The whole scene is funnier and darker than the main episode earns on its own.

jokes.text: The giant-object psychology reveal: Blake buys giant versions of everyday objects because his son disappeared while flying a giant kite — 'He's waiting for a better daddy, with a bigger hand.'
jokes.setup: Karen challenges Blake on his pattern of buying giant objects online
jokes.punchline: The reveal that the giant objects are connected to a lost son — who disappeared with a giant kite and 'they never found his body on the ground, which proves he's still up there waiting' — the deranged grief logic expressed through giant eBay purchases
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of Community's most memorable post-credits scenes. The logic chain is perfect dark absurdism: son flew giant kite → no body found on ground → therefore still airborne → still waiting → needs bigger hand to be caught by better daddy. Each step follows with its own horrible integrity. 'Which proves he's still up there waiting' as the conclusion from 'no body on the ground' is the kind of grief-logic that is both ridiculous and heartbreaking simultaneously. 'He's waiting for a better daddy, with a bigger hand' is an exceptional line — the specific, literal interpretation of what the son is waiting for, combined with the modest scale of Blake's ambition (just a bigger hand). The post-credits scene works as a mini-episode that reframes the entire main plot: the dean's giant hand was always someone's grief object; someone's loss funds another person's absurd problem. High originality, earned, deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: 'I thought it would look really cool.' (re: the giant watch)
jokes.setup: Karen has asked why he bought a giant watch when it has no connection to their missing son
jokes.punchline: Blake's honest admission breaks from the grief narrative entirely — the watch has no emotional significance, he just thought it would look cool, undercutting all the pathos
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion. The entire Blake scene has been building a profound-sounding mythos (giant objects = grief for lost son), and then Blake casually admits the watch has no such meaning — he just thought it'd look cool. The deflation of the pathos is the best possible punchline. Very economical, structurally perfect. 'I thought it would look really cool' as the last honest word on the subject before Karen walks the dog and eventually leaves is a beautiful dark comedy beat.

jokes.text: 'I'm gonna walk the dog, and eventually leave you.'
jokes.setup: Karen has heard Blake's admission about the watch; she decides to leave
jokes.punchline: 'Walk the dog, and eventually leave you' — the domestic chore and the life decision delivered in the same grammatical clause, with 'eventually' doing dark comedic work (not now, but sometime during this walk or after)
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. 'Walk the dog, and eventually leave you' is structurally flawless — the mundane ('walk the dog') and the devastating ('eventually leave you') share a single sentence with an 'and,' making the divorce an errand among errands. 'Eventually' is crucial: it implies she hasn't decided when, just that it'll happen, treating the marriage's end as a future calendar item. This is the kind of line that gets quoted forever. High originality, near-perfect economy, strong dark comedy. Approaches a 9 on craft, comparable to the best anchor examples.

jokes.text: 'I'll put the watch in the garage. And probably stop showering.'
jokes.setup: Karen has just said she's going to eventually leave him
jokes.punchline: Blake's response to impending divorce is to plan two things: (1) garage the watch, (2) stop showering — the second item is unexpected, final, and deeply funny as a portrait of a man already resigned to collapse
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Blake scene. 'Probably stop showering' as his plan for post-separation life is a small, specific detail that lands as both funny and genuinely sad. The 'probably' makes it funnier — not certain, still considering whether basic hygiene is worth maintaining. Extremely economical, great dark comedy, strong ending to the episode. 'And probably stop showering' ranks among the episode's most quotable lines.

tmdb_overview: A 19-foot plaster hand guides the group on an emotional journey as they travel through mountains and flashbacks while aboard Elroy's RV.
insight: RV-bound chaos delivers 65 jokes in 27 minutes—Community's densest episode yet.
